Let
\[
\Delta=2\theta+2\pi m
\]
be the required lifted angular change. Since \(m\ge 1\), we have \(\Delta>2\pi\).

The hyperbolic polar metric is
\[
ds^2=dr^2+\sinh^2 r\,d\lambda^2.
\]
The shortest admissible curve must wind around the forbidden disk \(r<\alpha\), so it consists of:

1. a geodesic tangent from \(P\) to the circle \(r=\alpha\),
2. an arc of the boundary circle \(r=\alpha\),
3. a geodesic tangent from the boundary circle to \(Q\).

For the right hyperbolic triangle with vertices \(O\), an endpoint at radius \(\beta\), and the tangent point on \(r=\alpha\), let \(\ell\) be the tangent segment length and \(\phi\) the angle at \(O\). Since the tangent meets \(r=\alpha\) orthogonally,
\[
\cosh \beta=\cosh\alpha\cosh\ell,
\]
so
\[
\ell=\operatorname{arcosh}\!\left(\frac{\cosh\beta}{\cosh\alpha}\right).
\]
Also the right-triangle relation gives
\[
\cos\phi=\frac{\tanh\alpha}{\tanh\beta},
\]
hence
\[
\phi=\arccos\!\left(\frac{\tanh\alpha}{\tanh\beta}\right).
\]

The two tangent segments account for angular change \(2\phi\), so the boundary arc must have angular length
\[
\Delta-2\phi.
\]
Since the boundary circle \(r=\alpha\) has metric length density \(\sinh\alpha\,d\lambda\), that arc has length
\[
\sinh\alpha(\Delta-2\phi).
\]

Therefore the minimum length is
\[
\boxed{
2\operatorname{arcosh}\!\left(\frac{\cosh\beta}{\cosh\alpha}\right)
+\sinh\alpha\left(2\theta+2\pi m
-2\arccos\!\left(\frac{\tanh\alpha}{\tanh\beta}\right)\right)
}.
\]

This is attained by the two tangent geodesic segments and the positively oriented boundary arc between their tangent points.
